transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Nimbus), Leah Kim (ML Eng, Nimbus), Carlos Ruiz (Infra Lead, Nimbus)

Agenda: 1) architecture differences (hosted vs dedicated) 2) perf tradeoffs (latency/throughput) 3) KV cache, batching, quantization behavior 4) VPC/on-prem isolation and guarantees 5) next steps / benchmark

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, i'll be the ae on this. priya from our se team will lead the technical portion, quick go round intros?
[00:18] Jordan: hey i'm jordan, cto at nimbus, thanks. our core ask is predictable latency for customer-facing features, and isolation because of compliance.
[00:32] Priya: nice to meet you all, i'll try to map how hosted vs dedicated behave on core vectors: tail latency, throughput, noisy neighbor risk, and operational controls like kv cache and batching.
[00:45] Leah: quick note — we have a 99th p90 latency target of 250ms for short chat completions (~150 tokens) and burst to 1k rps for search-ish workloads.
[01:05] Priya: got it — that's helpful. can i ask about auth and network constraints? you mentioned VPC earlier?
[01:18] Carlos: yes, networkwise we require private link / vpc peering for any customer data flow, and keys must integrate with our kms. also we may evaluate on-prem later.
[01:33] Alex: perfect, we'll surface private deployment options, ksm/hsm integration notes, etc. priya, i'll hand it to you.
[01:40] Priya: ok jumping in — first, high-level difference: hosted is multi-tenant with strong isolation boundaries logically; dedicated provides reserved GPU pools that give isolation at the resource level and predictable throughput because capacity isn't shared. hosted is lower friction and typically cheaper for variable workloads, but dedicated wins where isolation and predictable p99s are required.
[02:10] Priya: noisy neighbor question — on hosted we enforce scheduling and qps limits and reactive throttles; for strict noisy neighbor isolation we recommend dedicated where you own a pool (dedicated GPUs) so another tenant can't affect your VM/GPU. we also have tenancy-aware routing and soft limits for hosted.
[02:36] Jordan: do you guarantee throughput on dedicated? like can we sign for a committed baseline?
[02:44] Alex: yes — dedicated comes with reserved capacity and SLA-backed throughput targets. we can frame a commit for X GPUs / Y tokens per second and include burst policies. we'll share sample SLAs.
[02:58] Leah: ok, specifics: our workload is a mix: 60% short chat completions (<=150 tokens), 40% embedding-ish rerank that are short. we care about cold-start p99 and the steady-state throughput. how does kv cache help?
[03:18] Priya: KV cache reduces repeated compute for prefix contexts — for chat it can dramatically reduce tokens per request after warmup. in dedicated we can keep larger local kv caches longer, reducing cold-start impact. hosted caches are global and sharded; there is eviction based on capacity and workload.
[03:42] Priya: important: cache semantics — we keep per-session KV on the worker; if a request routes to a different worker and the kv isn't present, there is a miss and you pay the full compute for that chunk. dedicated reduces routing churn because you have sticky routing to your pool.
[04:05] Carlos: so for our session affinity — if we stick to dedicated, we get fewer kv misses?
[04:12] Priya: correct, dedicated + session affinity lowers kv miss rate, improves p99 for chat. hosted is still good for many apps but with noisy routing and more eviction pressure.
[04:25] Jordan: what about batching — we need low latency, does batching add unacceptable latency?
[04:33] Priya: batching helps throughput but can increase tail latency if you wait for a batch slot. Redwood's runtime does dynamic batching with latency SLOs; we will only batch up to a small window for latency-sensitive endpoints. on dedicated you can fine tune batch sizes and scheduler parameters to achieve your p99 target while maximizing throughput.
[04:55] Leah: can you quantify? like what's the added latency for a typical 10ms batch window?
[05:02] Priya: it depends on arrival patterns — a 10ms batching window adds ~10-15ms scheduling delay but can reduce GPU compute overhead per token by 20-40% depending on model and sequence length. we typically recommend microbatch windows of 5-20ms for sub-300ms SLOs.
[05:22] Jordan: and quantization — we use 4-bit and 8-bit model variants to save cost. how does Redwood handle quantized kernels and perf differences?
[05:30] Priya: runtime supports multiple quantization levels and chooses kernels accordingly. quantized models reduce memory and inference flops but may increase per-token latency slightly due to dequantize/requantize overhead on some ops; for most LLMs 8-bit gives near-native latency with big cost savings. 4-bit can give bigger cost reduction but may need extra calibration and can sometimes affect throughput for short sequences. we'll provide perf profiles for your target models.
[05:58] Alex: note — we'll share a benchmarking spreadsheet that shows p50/p90/p99 across model/quantization combos.
[06:06] Carlos: one risk is noisy neighbors even on dedicated if the infra VM hypervisor schedules badly. how do you mitigate noisy neighbor at infra level?
[06:16] Priya: dedicated pools map to isolated hosts or dedicated GPUs depending on the deployment. for onsite/private deployments we can pin GPUs, control cgroups, reserve pcie lanes, and isolate NICs. on hosted we rely on container runtime QoS, cgroup isolation, and hw topology-aware placement. dedicated customers also get priority preemption controls and can opt for full host reservations.
[06:44] Jordan: in terms of guarantees — can you commit to a sustained tokens-per-second per GPU baseline?
[06:52] Alex: yes, our dedicated contracts define baseline throughput per GPU and total pool capacity. the exact numbers depend on model/sequence length; we'll include model-specific throughput in the offer. for tight SLAs we recommend reserving an extra buffer (e.g., 10-20%) for headroom.
[07:10] Leah: how do you handle multi-region failover? we need cross-region fallback without leaking data.
[07:18] Priya: we support routing policies — primary region with encrypted cache and geo-fallback to a secondary region with customer agreement. data residency is enforced via VPC/private control plane and encryption at rest and in transit. for strict residency we recommend Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) where data never leaves your network.
[07:45] Carlos: sounds good. about the KV cache again — is it persistent across restarts or ephemeral?
[07:52] Priya: currently KV cache is in-memory on worker nodes and ephemeral; it's warmed via prefix caching and not persisted across node restarts. for some customers we offer a warmup service that preloads known conversation prefixes on deployment. for true persistence you'd pair with an external cache layer (we can integrate with customer's redis) — that increases complexity but guarantees persistence.
[08:18] Jordan: ok interesting. latencies — can you share typical p99 numbers for a mid-sized 7B model on dedicated vs hosted?
[08:30] Priya: rough numbers: hosted multi-tenant p99 for 150-token chat might be ~400-600ms depending on load; dedicated with reserved pool tuned for latency can get p99 down to ~200-300ms for similar config, subject to model and quantization. we'll put exact numbers in the benchmark sheet.
[08:51] Leah: any special kernel selection for quantized runs? we saw variable perf on different runtimes.
[08:58] Priya: runtime picks best kernels at startup and can recompile on the fly for certain ops; we choose vectorized int8/x4 kernels where available. kernel choice depends on hardware (A100 vs H100 vs Nvidia L4). for H100 we leverage transformer engine paths which improves latency for larger sequences.
[09:22] Alex: quick note on telemetry and observability — dedicated customers get per-model/per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and tracing hooks. we can also stream detailed traces for a sample period to your telemetry backend.
[09:36] Jordan: can we get logs that show cache hit/miss per session?
[09:40] Priya: yes we emit cache hit/miss metrics and per-route telemetry. retention and export depend on plan but we can export raw traces for a limited window for debugging.
[09:52] Carlos: what about model patching and rollouts — if we need to upgrade model versions in prod how do you avoid impacting latency?
[09:59] Priya: we support canary rollouts and traffic splitting at the route level. on dedicated you can provision parallel pools running different versions and shift traffic gradually. automatic fallback policies also allow instant rollback if latency/regression is detected.
[10:18] Leah: you mentioned auto-batching earlier; does the runtime batch across requests from different customers in hosted?
[10:25] Priya: yes hosted may batch across tenants when safe and beneficial, but we respect tenancy isolation boundaries; we do not co-mingle data in the same batch if tenants have strict isolation requirements. for dedicated you control pooling and batching and we'll avoid cross-tenant mixing entirely.
[10:46] Jordan: curious about on-prem — if we run your private deployment in our data center, do we get the same runtime features?
[10:55] Priya: almost feature parity. private deployments include the runtime, batching, kv cache, and kernel optimizations. differences: control plane is a customer-managed component; we provide admin tooling for rollouts and metrics export. KMS integration is local and audit logs are stored in your environment. some managed services like global routing and backup autoscaling are different or optional.
[11:22] Jordan: is there any feature you can't support on-prem?
[11:26] Priya: the hosted-only managed autoscaler that pulls from a global capacity pool isn't available on air-gapped installs, but we provide a robust autoscaler you can run inside your cluster. also some telemetry export to our SaaS console is optional if you want fully isolated operations.
[11:45] Carlos: okay i want to dig a bit into throughput guarantees under burst — if we have sudden 2x traffic spike, what happens?
[11:53] Alex: for dedicated you can provision burst capacity and policies; we offer two modes: strict reserved only (no burst, guaranteed baseline), or reserved with burst (we allow overflow onto spare capacity with best-effort latency). SLAs typically cover baseline and have best-effort for burst unless you contract extra buffer.
[12:18] Leah: for cost: how much delta between hosted and dedicated typically?
[12:23] Alex: depends — dedicated has a higher baseline cost because you reserve resources, but per-token unit cost can be lower with better packing and tuning. hosted is better for variable or low baseline workloads. we can model your expected cost with the benchmark traces.
[12:38] Priya: also don't forget engineer time: dedicated requires some ops input for topology and autoscaler rules, but we have templates.
[12:47] Jordan: benchmarks — we want an apples-to-apples run: our model, our sequence distribution, both hosted and dedicated configs. can you do that?
[12:55] Priya: yes we will: 1) you provide workload traces, 2) we'll provision a dedicated pool per agreed spec and run a 1-hour steady and burst window, and 3) we will run hosted tests with throttles configured similarly. results will include p50/p90/p99 and kv hit rates.
[13:17] Carlos: what about encryption/keys — in hosted are keys managed by Redwood? or can we bring-your-own-key (BYOK)?
[13:25] Alex: hosted supports BYOK via KMS integration for enterprise plans; private/dedicated always allow customer-managed KMS/HSM. we'll share our KMS integration guide.
[13:37] Leah: any compliance docs we can view?
[13:40] Alex: yes we'll send SOC2 type II summary, TLS/MTLS docs, and our data processing addendum.
[13:48] Jordan: quick nit — how does the runtime handle KV cache when a model rollout changes context window size?
[13:56] Priya: if you switch models with a different context window, existing kv entries might be incompatible; we recommend warming the new model's KV with known prefixes or running a rolling warmup. rollouts can be staged to avoid cold starts.
[14:18] Leah: let's talk about tooling — do you expose per-request debug headers we can use in prod to trace which worker served a request?
[14:25] Priya: yes, debug headers include worker id, cache hit boolean, and batch id for sampled requests. we can enable high sampling rates for short windows.
[14:38] Jordan: what about GPU types — we currently have H100s on our infra; will the runtime take advantage?
[14:44] Priya: yes, H100s are supported and we use transformer engine and optimized kernels for H100 which typically improves throughput and latency, especially for larger sequence lengths. we'll include model-specific numbers for H100 in the benchmark.
[14:58] Carlos: if we move to private on-prem, is the same kernel compiler available or do you have to rebuild?
[15:05] Priya: we supply the same binary/runtime optimized for common x86+NV setups; if you have very custom hardware we can provide a build with tuned kernels. most customers use our prebuilt images.
[15:22] Jordan: can you share sample config files for batcher tuning?
[15:26] Priya: yes — we'll include recommended config for latency-first and throughput-first profiles.
[15:33] Leah: are there any common gotchas you've seen?
[15:36] Priya: common gotchas: 1) forgetting session affinity increases kv misses; 2) over-quantizing before evals — 4-bit may change output quality; 3) not accounting for network egress costs in multi-region fallbacks; 4) not provisioning warmup for canaries.
[15:56] Alex: i'm going to open the doc links in the chat now (note: placeholder links) — architecture diagram: https://redwood.example/arch/dedicated-vs-hosted, benchmark template: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/template, security pack: https://redwood.example/security/soc2-summary
[16:12] Jordan: thanks — we'll look. question on autoscaling: does dedicated autoscaler rely on queue length or queue + GPU metrics?
[16:20] Priya: our autoscaler uses a combination: observed latency, queue length, GPU utilization, and custom business metrics. you can set policy thresholds (e.g., keep p99 under X ms).
[16:34] Carlos: if there's a degraded worker that's causing high p99, do you fail over requests?
[16:40] Priya: yes runtime marks unhealthy workers and reroutes traffic, and we have draining semantics to avoid in-flight KV loss. we also support instant fallback to a second pool for critical routes.
[16:53] Leah: what's the overhead for fallback? like if you fail to another region, how much added latency?
[16:59] Priya: cross-region adds network RTT — often 50-150ms depending on regions — so for latency-sensitive apps we recommend geo-provisioning or warm standby pools in the DR region.
[17:16] Jordan: do you have any case studies for customers with similar SLOs?
[17:22] Alex: yes, we'll include an anonymized case showing p99 reduction after moving to dedicated pools and adding kv affinity.
[17:30] Carlos: what about cost modeling — can you help simulate different reserved capacity levels?
[17:35] Alex: yes we'll run a cost model based on your traces and the benchmark results.
[17:42] Priya: quick note on model loading — larger models have longer cold-starts; if you expect intermittent spikes we recommend warm pools or smaller quantized variants for the burst tier.
[17:58] Leah: any recommended pilot size?
[18:02] Priya: typical pilot is 1-2 GPUs in a dedicated pool for 2-4 weeks with production traffic sampled at 1-5% to validate tail latency and kv hit rates.
[18:13] Jordan: okay let's capture next steps.
[18:18] Alex: action items / next steps: alex send pricing and security pack; priya run bench after leah provides traces; leah provide traces; schedule follow-up week of 6/23; we'll produce a benchmark report and recommended config.
[18:36] Jordan: sounds good. one last quick Q — SLA credits for missed p99?
[18:42] Alex: standard SLA credits apply for missed uptime/latency clauses in enterprise contract; we'll get legal to confirm language for throughput guarantees.
[18:55] Leah: thanks all — very helpful deep dive.
[19:00] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the deck and benchmark sheet.
